subject: What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF

messages.author: 929e733ff7821ad3
messages.subject: What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF
parts:
Dear all,

I am running a R-inla model with a 2D spde involved. My samples are not evenly distributed, so I expect that the estimated spatial random field outside the sampling area are caused by the imposed matern correlation structure and mesh structure. Sometimes, I do obtain hot/cold spots in areas where no samples exits (not in the outside area of the defined mesh). In an extreme case, the posterior mean of the whole random spatial field only contains hot/cold spot outside sampling area while the sampling area is more or less constant.

Can some experts give some hints about what could cause these strange hot/cold spots? And how should we interpret and treat it?

Thanks very much!

Regards,
Chun

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF
parts:
What kind of observation likelihood?
Sometimes nearby observations indicate a local spatial trend that gets extrapolated into regions with no observations. When this happens it can be a sign of a badly chosen model structure (in the sense that it doesn’t match with some aspects of the data generating mechanism). Har to tell without more details. Could you supply a picture of the type of effect you mention?

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF
parts:
Hi,
Those look like typical cases of extrapolated trends.
First thing to check: what do the uncertainty bands indicate? I.e., do the upper and lower quantiles diverge in opposite directions in those spots (which would be a good thing, showing that the model is uncertain about the values there) or do they both point in the same direction as the mean (indicating overfitting).

Finn

On 20 Sep 2018, at 21:05, lisa C <chunc...@gmail.com> wrote:

the likelihood is gaussian (observations are log-transformed positive densities). below is the spatial random field in levelplot. The big hot spot is right next to the samples where I would expect to have high densities (but I also have other covariates in the model to explain density, so I am not surprised if the sample area does not show any signals). However, I am surprised to see hot spots next to the samples.

thanks
